description: Düzce Üniversitesi Bilgisayar Mühendisliği öğrencisi 4 yazılım meraklısı olarak uzay teknolojilerine olan ilgimizi somut bir projeye dönüştürmek için bir aradayız. Python, web/mobil geliştirme, veri analizi ve sistem tasarımı alanlarındaki teknik altyapımızı güçlü ekip uyumumuzla birleştiriyoruz. Kadromuz tamam; disiplinli çalışmamız ve üretme heyecanımızla NASA Space Apps Challenge’da fark yaratmaya hazırız.
summary:
We developed AutoSpace, a 100% offline-capable autonomous physiological digital twin and medical decision-support platform designed for deep space missions. On long-duration journeys to Mars, communication latency with Earth reaches up to 21 minutes one-way (42 minutes round-trip), making real-time telemedicine impossible during acute medical crises such as solar particle radiation storms, Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), jugular vein thrombosis, microgravity thermal overload, and cognitive isolation stress. 

Calibrated with NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) baselines and NASA-STD-3001 clinical thresholds, AutoSpace continuously fuses multi-organ biometric telemetry, filters cosmic-ray-induced sensor bit-flip anomalies, predicts critical threshold breaches in advance, and autonomously prescribes closed-loop countermeasures alongside automated EVA (GO/NO-GO) safety clearance. By minimizing manual interpretation and human error under high stress, AutoSpace enables Earth-Independent Medical Operations (EIMO) for deep space pioneers while also providing life-saving autonomous triage for remote, offline clinics and disaster zones on Earth.
details:
Project Details

1. What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

AutoSpace is an astronaut digital twin that monitors astronaut health in real time during deep-space missions, performs organ-based risk analysis, and provides autonomous decision support to the crew when communication with Earth is limited or delayed.

  • Data Collection and Analysis: The system fuses simulated (or real storm-recorded) physiological and environmental sensor data on board in real time.
  • Risk Engine: It compares this data every second against critical thresholds defined in NASA-STD-3001 and NASA HRP (Human Research Program) standards, visualizing organ-level statuses (eye/SANS, brain, heart, bone marrow, etc.) using green, yellow, and red risk tiers.
  • Autonomous Decision-Making (GO / NO-GO): Whenever a risk threshold is exceeded or a sudden solar storm or solar energetic particle (SEP) event begins, the system generates autonomous decisions. It alerts astronauts with "NO-GO" or "CAUTION" statuses and displays step-by-step emergency action protocols (such as moving to a radiation storm shelter or applying LBNP at −25 mmHg).
  • "What-If" Planner: Before a scheduled extravehicular activity (EVA) or resistance exercise (ARED), it predicts whether the activity is safe based on current radiation and biological load projections.

2. What Are Its Benefits?

  • Saves Time (Saves Lives): On a mission to Mars, one-way communication delay with Earth ranges from 4 to 24 minutes (modeled as 21 minutes in the demo), meaning receiving medical guidance from Earth during an emergency can take over 40 minutes. AutoSpace operates locally and autonomously, reducing response time to milliseconds.
  • Uninterrupted Offline Reliability: Even if the backend server or connection to Earth is lost, the system continues to operate 100% offline via an identical JavaScript decision engine running directly in the browser.
  • Comprehensive Biomonitoring: Beyond standard vital signs, it covers critical space-specific health risks such as SANS (Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome), jugular vein thrombosis, space anemia, thermal load, and cabin microbiome health.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

The core goal of AutoSpace is to bring NASA's EIMO (Earth-Independent Medical Operations) vision to life. By reducing the crew's reliance on ground control, it empowers astronauts—even without a dedicated flight surgeon on board—to manage complex health and environmental threats autonomously and safely.

4. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS (for a modern, responsive interface), Recharts (for dynamic health telemetry charts), and Lucide (for UI icons).
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI (high-performance REST API), Pydantic (data validation), and SQLite (fast offline caching).
  • Voice Interface: Web Speech API for hands-free voice commands and automated spoken alerts.
  • Data Sources: NASA DONKI (space weather events), NASA OSDR (personal biomarker baselines), NASA PDS (Curiosity RAD dosimetry data), and NOAA GOES satellite proton flux datasets.

5. How Creative Is Your Project?

  • Dual-Engine Architecture: If the backend crashes or becomes unreachable, the frontend seamlessly switches within seconds to a local JavaScript decision engine running the exact same rules, ensuring zero downtime.
  • Astronaut Digital Twin: Rather than relying solely on raw charts, it visualizes the entire body map through a live, holistic digital twin, translating complex medical telemetry into clear, actionable insights.
  • Realistic Delay & Comms Queue System: Simulating Earth communications through a realistic 21-minute delayed message queue elevates the scientific realism of deep-space mission operations.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • Harsh Deep-Space Conditions: Real space physiology challenges—including solar particle events (SEP) and microgravity-induced fluid shifts affecting ocular and circulatory systems (such as SANS)—were factored into the models.
  • Psychological and Cognitive Load: To prevent crew panic during emergencies, step-by-step Action Cards and hands-free voice controls were designed for rapid, low-stress execution.
  • Data Reliability: Instead of arbitrary or estimated thresholds, official NASA-STD-3001 limits and peer-reviewed spaceflight datasets were used as the foundation for all calculations.
